Calvient
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P
Page 1
April 14, 2026
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
Department of Health and Human Services
Attention: CMS-0062-P
P.O. Box 8013
Baltimore, MD 21244-8013
Re: 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P)
Dear Administrator Becerra and CMS Staff:
I. Introduction and Interest of Calvient
Calvient appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed rule CMS-
0062-P, the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Proposed Rule. We commend CMS for taking this critical step to extend electronic prior 
authorization requirements to prescription drugs, building on the foundation established 
by the CMS-0057-F final rule.
Calvient is a healthcare technology company that develops AI-powered solutions for 
prior authorizations, inbound and outbound referrals, intelligent document processing, 
fax management, and healthcare operations automation. Our platform serves federally 
qualified health centers (FQHCs), community health centers, and health systems across 
the United States. These organizations operate on the front lines of patient care delivery 
for some of the most underserved populations in the country, and they experience the 
burden of prior authorization more acutely than almost any other segment of the 
healthcare system.
We write from the perspective of a technology company that works daily with providers 
who are, in their own words, drowning in prior authorization requests. Our comments 
are informed by direct experience automating PA workflows, processing unstructured 
clinical documentation, and interfacing with the payer systems that administer these 
requirements. We strongly support the direction of this proposed rule while urging CMS 
to go further in addressing the root causes of administrative burden.
II. General Support for the Proposed Rule
Calvient supports the core objectives of CMS-0062-P. Extending the interoperability and 
prior authorization framework to prescription drugs is overdue and essential. Drug prior 
authorization represents a significant and growing share of the administrative burden 
borne by providers, and the absence of electronic standards for drug PA has left 
providers reliant on fragmented, manual processes that delay patient access to 
necessary medications.
We specifically support the following provisions:
Calvient
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P
Page 2
Compressed decision timeframes. The proposed 24-hour urgent and 72-hour 
standard decision windows are appropriate and reflect the clinical reality that drug prior 
authorization delays can directly harm patients. When a patient at an FQHC is 
prescribed a medication that requires prior authorization, every day of delay is a day 
that patient goes without treatment. The current timeframes are inadequate, and we 
commend CMS for proposing meaningful compression.
Mandatory electronic PA via FHIR and NCPDP standards. The adoption of HL7 
FHIR-based standards for drugs covered under medical benefits and NCPDP SCRIPT, 
Formulary & Benefit, and Real-Time Prescription Benefit standards for pharmacy 
benefits is a critical infrastructure investment. These standards create the foundation for 
automated, interoperable PA workflows. We particularly welcome the adoption of the Da 
Vinci Prior Authorization Support (PAS), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), 
and Clinical Data Exchange (CDex) implementation guides, which we discuss in detail 
below.
Specific denial reasons. Requiring payers to provide specific reasons when denying a 
drug PA request is essential for providers to understand what additional documentation 
or clinical justification is needed, and to mount effective appeals. Vague denials waste 
provider time and delay patient care.
Public reporting of PA metrics. Transparency in approval rates, denial rates, and 
turnaround times will create accountability and enable providers to make informed 
decisions about payer performance. We encourage CMS to ensure these metrics are 
reported in a standardized, machine-readable format to enable meaningful comparison.
III. The Fax Is Not the Problem: Addressing the True Source of 
Administrative Burden
While we strongly support the move to electronic standards, we urge CMS to recognize 
that the transmission medium is only one dimension of the prior authorization burden. 
The fax is not the problem. The problem is the intensity, variability, and volume of 
the documentation requirements themselves.
Our clients at FQHCs and health systems consistently report that the most time-
consuming aspect of prior authorization is not the act of submitting a request, whether 
by fax, phone, portal, or API. It is the work required to complete the payer-specific 
questionnaires and gather the clinical documentation necessary to satisfy each payer's 
unique requirements. These questionnaires are often lengthy, clinically intensive, and 
vary significantly from payer to payer, even for the same drug and the same clinical 
indication.
Consider the workflow a provider faces today when a prior authorization is triggered:
First, the provider must determine whether a prior authorization is even required for the 
specific drug, for the specific patient, under the specific plan. This determination is often 
not straightforward and may require calling the payer or checking a portal.
Calvient
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P
Page 3
Second, the provider must locate the correct questionnaire or documentation 
requirements for that payer and that drug. These requirements are not standardized. 
One payer may require a two-page form; another may require a twelve-page clinical 
questionnaire with detailed lab values, prior treatment history, specialist notes, and 
clinical justification narratives.
Third, the provider's staff must scrub the patient's chart to extract the relevant clinical 
data points: lab results, diagnosis codes, medication history, specialist consult notes, 
imaging results, and more. This data often resides in different parts of the EHR, in 
scanned documents, or in records from other providers that may not be in the system at 
all.
Fourth, the staff must complete the questionnaire, compile supporting documentation, 
and submit the package. Even with electronic submission, this process routinely 
requires 30 to 60 minutes per request for complex medications, and many providers 
process dozens of these daily.
Fifth, the provider must then monitor the status of the request, respond to additional 
information requests from the payer, and manage appeals when requests are denied.
The result is that many FQHCs and health systems employ full-time staff whose sole 
responsibility is managing prior authorizations. According to the American Medical 
Association, physicians complete an average of 39 to 43 prior authorization requests 
per week, requiring 13 to 16 hours of physician and staff time. Ninety-three percent of 
physicians report that prior authorization delays patient care, and 89 percent say it 
contributes to clinician burnout. These numbers are even more acute at safety-net 
providers like FQHCs, where staffing is already constrained and the patient population 
often faces the greatest barriers to medication access.
Moving from fax to API does not solve this problem. It makes the submission faster, but 
the work of preparing the submission remains the bottleneck.
IV. The Da Vinci DTR Standard and the Role of AI-Augmented 
Workflows
This is why the proposed adoption of the Da Vinci Documentation Templates and Rules 
(DTR) implementation guide is, in our view, the most consequential element of this rule, 
and why CMS should give it particular emphasis in the final rule.
DTR enables payers to publish their documentation requirements and coverage rules in 
a structured, machine-readable format that can be executed within the provider's 
workflow. Rather than requiring a staff member to locate a PDF questionnaire, manually 
interpret the questions, search the chart for relevant data, and type in answers, DTR 
allows the documentation requirements to be delivered electronically and, critically, 
allows supporting data to be pre-populated from the patient's clinical record.
This is where we urge CMS to look forward and recognize the AI-augmented future that 
is already emerging in healthcare operations.
Calvient
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P
Page 4
Today, a growing number of healthcare organizations are deploying AI agents that 
assist clinical and administrative staff with the prior authorization workflow. These AI 
agents do not replace human judgment. They augment human capabilities and 
efficiency by performing the labor-intensive preparatory work that consumes the 
majority of PA processing time:
Chart scrubbing: AI agents can review a patient's clinical record, identify the data 
points relevant to a specific payer's documentation requirements, and extract lab 
values, diagnosis histories, medication lists, and specialist notes from structured and 
unstructured sources within the EHR.
Questionnaire completion: When payer documentation requirements are delivered in 
a structured format via DTR, AI agents can map extracted clinical data to the specific 
fields and questions in the payer's questionnaire, pre-populating answers for human 
review and approval.
Necessity verification: AI agents can cross-reference the prescribed drug against the 
payer's formulary and coverage criteria to determine whether prior authorization is 
required at all, and if so, whether the patient's clinical profile is likely to meet the 
approval criteria, before the staff invests time in completing the submission.
Status monitoring and follow-up: Through PAS APIs, AI agents can track the status 
of submitted requests, flag pending items requiring attention, and assist staff in 
preparing responses to payer requests for additional information.
Supporting documentation assembly: Using CDex, AI agents can compile and 
format the clinical attachments that accompany PA requests, including C-CDA 
documents, PDFs, and clinical narratives, ensuring completeness before submission.
This is not a speculative future. These capabilities exist today and are being deployed at 
health systems and FQHCs across the country. The question before CMS is whether 
the electronic prior authorization framework it establishes through this rule will be 
designed to facilitate this kind of AI-augmented workflow, or whether it will inadvertently 
create barriers to it.
V. Specific Recommendations
Based on our experience serving FQHCs and health systems, and our understanding of 
the current and emerging capabilities of AI-augmented PA workflows, we offer the 
following recommendations:
1. Mandate DTR adoption with the same urgency as PAS
The proposed rule requires payers to support electronic prior authorization submission 
(PAS) and clinical data exchange (CDex) for drugs. We urge CMS to place equal 
emphasis on requiring payers to publish their drug coverage requirements and 
documentation questionnaires in structured, machine-readable DTR format. Without 
DTR, electronic submission still requires providers to manually determine what 
documentation is needed. With DTR, both human staff and AI-assisted tools can 
Calvient
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P
Page 5
programmatically discover the payer's requirements and map clinical data to those 
requirements. This is the difference between making the fax electronic and actually 
reducing the work.
2. Require payers to expose PA necessity determination via API
A significant amount of wasted effort occurs because providers cannot easily determine 
whether a prior authorization is required for a specific drug, for a specific patient, under 
a specific plan. We recommend CMS require impacted payers to expose a real-time API 
endpoint that allows providers (and their technology systems) to query whether PA is 
required before initiating the documentation and submission process. The Real-Time 
Prescription Benefit (RTPB) standard is a step in this direction, but CMS should make 
explicit that PA necessity determination is a required capability, not merely a benefit 
check.
3. Establish standards for questionnaire consistency and complexity limits
Even with structured DTR delivery, the variability and complexity of payer 
questionnaires remains a major burden driver. We recommend CMS work with payers, 
providers, and standards bodies to develop guidelines for questionnaire design that 
promote consistency across payers for the same drug categories, limit the length and 
complexity of questionnaires to what is clinically necessary for the coverage 
determination, and ensure questions are answerable using data routinely captured in 
standard clinical workflows. The goal should be to reduce the total cognitive and labor 
burden of PA completion, not merely to digitize the current burden.
4. Design the EPA framework to support AI-augmented workflows
We urge CMS to acknowledge in the final rule that the electronic prior authorization 
(EPA) process should be designed to accommodate AI-augmented workflows alongside 
human-driven ones. This does not mean delegating clinical decision-making to 
machines. It means recognizing that AI agents are already assisting providers by 
scrubbing charts, pre-populating documentation, identifying missing data, and 
monitoring submission status, and that the standards and API requirements should 
facilitate rather than impede this assistance.
Specifically, we recommend that CMS ensure DTR questionnaires are delivered in 
formats that are both human-readable and machine-processable, that PAS APIs 
support programmatic status queries at reasonable polling intervals to enable 
automated status monitoring, that CDex attachment specifications support automated 
compilation of clinical documents from EHR data, and that payer API rate limits and 
access policies accommodate the throughput requirements of organizations processing 
high volumes of PA requests with technology assistance.
5. Address the unique needs of FQHCs and safety-net providers
FQHCs serve over 30 million patients annually, disproportionately from Medicaid, 
uninsured, and underserved populations. These organizations face the same PA 
Calvient
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P
Page 6
requirements as large health systems but with significantly fewer resources. The 
proposed rule's extension of requirements to Medicaid managed care plans and CHIP 
programs is particularly relevant to FQHCs.
We recommend that CMS consider providing technical assistance or funding to support 
FQHCs in adopting the FHIR-based systems needed to take advantage of electronic 
PA, that small health plan compliance timelines (36 months) be paired with 
requirements that those plans begin making DTR questionnaires available to providers 
on an accelerated timeline even before full API compliance, and that CMS monitor 
whether the rule's benefits are reaching safety-net providers or whether they are 
accruing primarily to large health systems with greater technical capacity.
VI. Response to Requests for Information
Step Therapy Processes
Step therapy requirements compound the prior authorization burden by requiring 
providers to document failed trials of alternative therapies before a preferred medication 
can be authorized. We encourage CMS to consider requiring payers to publish step 
therapy protocols in structured, machine-readable formats alongside their DTR 
questionnaires, so that providers and their technology systems can programmatically 
determine step therapy requirements and document compliance. This would 
significantly reduce the back-and-forth that currently characterizes step therapy 
workflows.
Prior Authorization Burden for Laboratory Tests and DME
We strongly encourage CMS to extend the interoperability framework to laboratory tests 
and durable medical equipment in future rulemaking. These categories represent a 
substantial and growing PA burden for our provider clients. The same principles we 
advocate in this comment, including structured questionnaire delivery via DTR, 
necessity determination via API, and support for AI-augmented workflows, should apply 
to these categories as well.
VII. Conclusion
CMS-0062-P represents a significant and welcome step toward reducing the prior 
authorization burden for prescription drugs. We urge CMS to finalize this rule and to 
strengthen it by addressing not just the transmission medium, but the underlying 
complexity and variability of documentation requirements that consume the majority of 
provider time and resources.
We are entering an era where AI-augmented workflows can dramatically reduce 
administrative burden without replacing human clinical judgment. The electronic prior 
authorization framework CMS establishes through this rule will shape whether that 
potential is realized. We respectfully urge CMS to design the EPA process with this 
future in mind: structured, machine-readable documentation requirements; real-time 
Calvient
Public Comment on CMS-0062-P
Page 7
necessity determination; programmatic status monitoring; and API architectures that 
support both human and AI-assisted interactions.
The providers we serve at FQHCs and health systems are not asking for less 
accountability in the prior authorization process. They are asking for a process that 
respects their time, their patients' needs, and the reality that technology can and should 
make this work more efficient. CMS-0062-P is an opportunity to deliver on that promise.
Calvient welcomes the opportunity to serve as a resource to CMS as it finalizes this 
rule. We would be pleased to provide demonstrations of AI-augmented PA workflows, 
share anonymized data on PA processing times and outcomes, or participate in any 
stakeholder engagement process CMS may convene.
Respectfully submitted,
Jonathan Minson
CEO
Calvient
administration@calvient.com
https://www.calvient.com
analysis:
**1. COMMENTER INFORMATION**
- Author/Organization name: Calvient (Jonathan Minson, CEO)
- Stakeholder type: Technology Vendor
- Credentials or expertise mentioned: Healthcare technology company developing AI-powered solutions for prior authorizations, referrals, intelligent document processing, and healthcare operations automation. Platform serves federally qualified health centers (FQHCs), community health centers, and health systems across the United States.

**2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**
Calvient strongly supports CMS-0062-P's extension of electronic prior authorization requirements to prescription drugs but urges CMS to address the root cause of administrative burden: the complexity and variability of documentation requirements, not just the transmission medium. The company advocates for mandatory adoption of the Da Vinci DTR standard, real-time PA necessity determination APIs, and designing the EPA framework to support AI-augmented workflows that can dramatically reduce provider burden while maintaining human clinical judgment.

**3. REGULATORY CONTEXT**
- Specific sections/provisions addressed: CMS-0062-P (2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule), building on CMS-0057-F final rule
- Regulatory citations mentioned: Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP programs, 24-hour urgent and 72-hour standard decision windows
- Standards referenced: HL7 FHIR, NCPDP SCRIPT, Formulary & Benefit, Real-Time Prescription Benefit (RTPB), Da Vinci Prior Authorization Support (PAS), Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), Clinical Data Exchange (CDex), C-CDA

**4. DETAILED POSITIONS**

Topic: Compressed Decision Timeframes
- Position: Support
- Rationale: 24-hour urgent and 72-hour standard windows reflect clinical reality that drug PA delays directly harm patients, especially at FQHCs
- Specific request: Finalize proposed timeframes

Topic: Mandatory Electronic PA via FHIR and NCPDP Standards
- Position: Support
- Rationale: Creates foundation for automated, interoperable PA workflows; particularly welcome Da Vinci PAS, DTR, and CDex implementation guides
- Specific request: Finalize standards adoption

Topic: Specific Denial Reasons
- Position: Support
- Rationale: Essential for providers to understand what additional documentation is needed and to mount effective appeals; vague denials waste time
- Specific request: Require payers to provide specific denial reasons

Topic: Public Reporting of PA Metrics
- Position: Support with Enhancement
- Rationale: Transparency creates accountability and enables informed decisions about payer performance
- Specific request: Ensure metrics are reported in standardized, machine-readable format

Topic: Da Vinci DTR Standard Adoption
- Position: Strongly Support with Enhancement
- Rationale: DTR is the most consequential element of the rule; enables structured, machine-readable documentation requirements that can be pre-populated from clinical records
- Specific request: Mandate DTR adoption with same urgency as PAS; place equal emphasis on requiring payers to publish drug coverage requirements in DTR format

Topic: PA Necessity Determination via API
- Position: Modify/Add
- Rationale: Significant wasted effort occurs determining if PA is required; RTPB is a step but insufficient
- Specific request: Require payers to expose real-time API endpoint for PA necessity queries

Topic: Questionnaire Consistency and Complexity Limits
- Position: Add New Requirement
- Rationale: Variability and complexity of payer questionnaires remains major burden driver even with DTR
- Specific request: Develop guidelines promoting consistency across payers, limiting questionnaire length/complexity to clinical necessity

Topic: AI-Augmented Workflows Support
- Position: Add Framework Consideration
- Rationale: AI agents already assisting providers with chart scrubbing, pre-population, status monitoring; standards should facilitate not impede
- Specific request: Design EPA to accommodate AI-augmented workflows; ensure DTR is machine-processable, PAS supports programmatic queries, CDex supports automated compilation, API rate limits accommodate high-volume processing

Topic: FQHC and Safety-Net Provider Support
- Position: Add Support Provisions
- Rationale: FQHCs serve 30+ million patients with significantly fewer resources than large health systems
- Specific request: Provide technical assistance/funding for FHIR adoption; accelerate DTR questionnaire availability timeline; monitor whether benefits reach safety-net providers

Topic: Step Therapy Processes
- Position: Add Structured Format Requirement
- Rationale: Step therapy compounds PA burden; structured formats would reduce back-and-forth
- Specific request: Require payers to publish step therapy protocols in machine-readable formats alongside DTR questionnaires

Topic: PA for Laboratory Tests and DME
- Position: Support Future Extension
- Rationale: Represent substantial and growing PA burden
- Specific request: Extend interoperability framework to lab tests and DME in future rulemaking

**5. RECOMMENDATIONS**
1. Mandate DTR adoption with the same urgency as PAS, requiring payers to publish drug coverage requirements and documentation questionnaires in structured, machine-readable DTR format
2. Require payers to expose PA necessity determination via real-time API endpoint
3. Establish standards for questionnaire consistency and complexity limits, working with payers, providers, and standards bodies
4. Design the EPA framework to support AI-augmented workflows, ensuring DTR is machine-processable, PAS supports programmatic queries, CDex supports automated compilation, and API rate limits accommodate high-volume processing
5. Address unique needs of FQHCs and safety-net providers through technical assistance/funding, accelerated DTR timelines, and monitoring of benefit distribution
6. Require payers to publish step therapy protocols in structured, machine-readable formats
7. Extend interoperability framework to laboratory tests and durable medical equipment in future rulemaking

**6. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS**

Primary Concerns:
- Electronic submission alone does not reduce administrative burden; the work of preparing submissions remains the bottleneck
- Complexity and variability of payer-specific documentation requirements consume majority of PA processing time (30-60 minutes per complex request)
- Providers cannot easily determine if PA is required for specific drug/patient/plan combinations
- Questionnaires vary significantly payer-to-payer even for same drug and clinical indication
- One payer may require 2-page form while another requires 12-page clinical questionnaire
- Chart scrubbing requires extracting data from different EHR locations, scanned documents, external records

Potential Negative Impacts:
- FQHCs and safety-net providers may lack technical capacity to benefit from electronic PA if support not provided
- Benefits may accrue primarily to large health systems with greater technical resources
- Without DTR, electronic submission still requires manual determination of documentation needs
- API rate limits and access policies may not accommodate high-volume PA processing needs

Implementation Barriers:
- Many FQHCs employ full-time staff solely for managing prior authorizations
- Physicians complete average 39-43 PA requests per week requiring 13-16 hours of staff time (AMA data)
- 93% of physicians report PA delays patient care; 89% say it contributes to burnout
- Safety-net providers have constrained staffing and patients face greatest barriers to medication access
- Small health plans have 36-month compliance timeline which may delay benefits

**7. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE**

Data/Statistics Cited:
- American Medical Association: Physicians complete average of 39-43 prior authorization requests per week
- AMA: PA requires 13-16 hours of physician and staff time per week
- AMA: 93% of physicians report PA delays patient care
- AMA: 89% of physicians say PA contributes to clinician burnout
- FQHCs serve over 30 million patients annually
- FQHC patients disproportionately from Medicaid, uninsured, and underserved populations
- Complex medication PA requests routinely require 30-60 minutes per request
- Many providers process dozens of PA requests daily

Studies/Research Referenced:
- American Medical Association research on PA burden

Examples Provided:
- Five-step workflow providers face when PA is triggered: (1) determine if PA required, (2) locate correct questionnaire, (3) scrub patient chart for data, (4) complete questionnaire and submit, (5) monitor status and manage appeals
- AI agent capabilities: chart scrubbing, questionnaire completion, necessity verification, status monitoring, documentation assembly
- Variability example: one payer requires 2-page form, another requires 12-page questionnaire with lab values, treatment history, specialist notes, clinical narratives

**8. IMPACT ASSESSMENT**

Affected Stakeholders:
- Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) and community health centers
- Health systems
- Healthcare providers (physicians and clinical staff)
- Safety-net providers
- Patients in underserved populations
- Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries
- Payers (health plans)
- Technology vendors

Economic Implications:
- Reduced administrative costs through automation of chart scrubbing, questionnaire completion, status monitoring
- Decreased physician/staff time burden (currently 13-16 hours/week)
- Potential need for technical assistance/funding for FQHCs
- Cost savings from reducing 30-60 minute processing time per complex request
- Full-time staff dedicated to PA management could be redeployed

Technical Feasibility:
- AI-augmented workflows already deployed at health systems and FQHCs
- Capabilities exist today for chart scrubbing, pre-population, status monitoring, documentation assembly
- FHIR, NCPDP, Da Vinci PAS, DTR, and CDex standards provide technical foundation
- Concerns about API rate limits, access policies, and technical capacity at small providers
- Small health plans have 36-month compliance timeline

Patient Care Impact:
- Reduced medication access delays
- Every day of PA delay means patients go without treatment
- Particularly acute for FQHC patients facing greatest barriers to medication access
- 93% of physicians report current PA delays patient care
- Improved care quality through faster access to necessary medications
- Reduced clinician burnout (89% cite PA as contributor) improves care quality

**9. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS**
- Overall position: Supportive with Significant Enhancement Recommendations
- Tone: Professional, Technical, Collaborative, Evidence-Based
- Priority level: High

**10. KEY QUOTES**

"The fax is not the problem. The problem is the intensity, variability, and volume of the documentation requirements themselves." (Page 2) - Emphasizes that electronic transmission alone doesn't solve administrative burden

"Moving from fax to API does not solve this problem. It makes the submission faster, but the work of preparing the submission remains the bottleneck." (Page 3) - Core argument that documentation preparation is the real burden

"This is why the proposed adoption of the Da Vinci Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR) implementation guide is, in our view, the most consequential element of this rule." (Page 4) - Identifies DTR as critical component

"We are entering an era where AI-augmented workflows can dramatically reduce administrative burden without replacing human clinical judgment. The electronic prior authorization framework CMS establishes through this rule will shape whether that potential is realized." (Page 6-7) - Vision for AI-assisted future of PA processing

**11. THEMES**
- Interoperability (primary focus: FHIR, NCPDP, Da Vinci standards)
- Provider Burden (primary focus: administrative time, workflow efficiency)
- AI/ML (primary focus: AI-augmented workflows, automation)
- Implementation Timeline (concern for small plans, FQHCs)
- Health Equity (focus on FQHCs, safety-net providers, underserved populations)
- Patient Access (medication access delays)
- Cost/Resources (staff time, technical capacity, funding needs)
- Certification (standards adoption, API requirements)
- Technology Standards (DTR, PAS, CDex, RTPB)
- Transparency/Accountability (public reporting of PA metrics)
